fuzzy.prompt: what happens to old transaction records on the streaming side once they get too old?
fuzzy.native_answer:
Old records aren't archived by the streaming layer — Kafka deletes them. What I can confirm from what I have on this cluster:

Per-topic retention (decided 2026-08-14)
- evt.payments.* → 21 days per-topic (set that way because audit needs 21 days; longer replay was wanted but 21d was the call).
- All other topics → broker default. I don't have the default's retention.ms value recorded, so I won't guess the number — that's a `kafka-configs.sh --describe` / broker config lookup.

What deletion actually looks like
- Deletion is segment-granular, not record-granular: log segments roll on segment.ms/segment.bytes, and a segment is only eligible once its newest record is past retention.ms (or the log exceeds retention.bytes). So real-world retention can overshoot the configured window by up to one segment's worth of traffic.
- The active segment is never deleted, so a busy partition effectively keeps at least one segment regardless.
- Deletion is silent and unrecoverable from Kafka's side — there's no tombstone for "this got aged out."

Consequences worth keeping in mind
- The 21-day window IS the replay budget. A consumer group that falls further behind than retention, or that gets reset to a stale committed offset, hits OffsetOutOfRange; recovery is auto.offset.reset (earliest/latest) or a manual seek, and with earliest you don't get the oldest records back — you get whatever survived in retention.
- Long-term history for payments lives in whatever the sink wrote (e.g. svc.payments.ledger-writer downstream store), not in the topic. If the audit requirement is 21 days on the topic, the durable copy has to exist downstream.
- Retention is unrelated to offset retention for consumer groups (offsets.retention.minutes), which is a separate clock — worth not conflating the two.

Sept 14 was the auth (sign-in) restart storm — a 22-minute incident, self-inflicted by the health checks.

What happened, in order:

- The liveness probe for the auth service wasn't just checking "is this process alive" — it called the user-database as part of its check.
- The database had a latency spike. The probe calls started timing out.
- Kubelet read those timeouts as "the container is dead" and killed and restarted every auth pod.
- That's the amplification: the pods going down didn't fix the DB. New pods came up, immediately probed the same slow database, failed the same way, and got killed again. Every restart also threw cold-start load at the DB, so the latency got worse and the loop fed itself.

The fix was a separation of concerns: the dependency check (user-database) was moved out of the liveness probe and into the readiness probe only. Liveness is now a plain port check, so a slow dependency takes a pod out of rotation instead of getting it killed. That's the general postmortem rule we adopted: anything that touches a dependency belongs in readiness, never liveness — and no new probe is allowed to use the default `timeoutSeconds: 1`.

The rule we settled on: a pod reports healthy in two separate ways, and dependency checks belong only in the second one.

- Liveness = "is this process alive" — a plain port check on the container itself, nothing else. It must never touch a dependency, because failing liveness is what triggers kubelet to kill the pod.
- Readiness = "can this pod serve traffic right now" — this is where any check that reaches a dependency (DB, cache, downstream service) lives. A failing readiness just pulls the pod out of the load balancer; it doesn't restart anything.
